I ordered the Steam Link when it was on sale about a month ago--didn't get the Steam Controller at the time. I ended up really liking the Link so when the Steam Summer Sale hit, I went ahead and snagged a controller while it was $35.

I'm not much of a console gamer, but I do have an XBox One and play a few games on it sometimes (I only get the free games with my Gold subscription). I'm marginally competent with a controller, although I far prefer gaming on a PC with keyboard & mouse. That said, I enjoyed having my Steam library available on my TV and I really wanted to see if a controller would work for me.

The Steam Controller is a classic bat-wing style console controller, but not as comfortable as my XBox One. It comes with a dongle that you can plug into your Link (or your computer) that allows you to go wireless, or you can attach it with a USB (tested on my PC but not the Link). It has a few unique features that any review will point out, so I'll just touch on them briefly.

First is the touch pad on the right hand side that emulates a mouse. You use it in conjunction with a standard mini joystick on the left for movement. In FPS terms, the touch pad allows you to mouse-look and the mini joystick is your WSAD. I tested this on a few games with mixed results. It worked very well in slow moving games like The Vanishing of Ethan Carter and Dear Esther, but worked poorly in FPSs that require twitch reflexes (like Serious Sam HD, Doom, and even the more leisurely paced A Story About My Uncle). The issue with the touchpad is sensitivity and limited area....even with the sensitivity dialed down, dragging your thumb across the pad whips you around. Unfortunately the touch pad is only about the size of a silver dollar so it's not uncommon to have to pick up your thumb when you hit the edge and jump back over to the other side.

The other unique thing about the Steam Controller are key bindings and custom configurations. You can bind anything on the controller to any keyboard command from within Steam in Big Picture Mode. It's very simple. Also, almost all games have either a developer provided controller configuration available and/or tons of configs from the community that you can select. You can easily discern which are the most popular.

Other than the aforementioned games I've listed, I've also used it extensively with Limbo. This is a platformer with a very limited control scheme. The controller is PERFECT for this type of game. I also tested it with South Park: The Stick of Truth. It worked fine for that as well.

I had previously tried my XBox One controller with the Link and it worked fine--it just had to be connected via USB. I believe you can use a PS4 controller wireless. Is the Steam Controller worth buying? Yes, but with caveats. If you already have a wireless controller that will work with the Link, I wouldn't bother, but if you don't then get it while it's on sale. You will not be able to competitively game in FPSs with it, however it works great for RPGs, platformers, turn-based strategy, walking-sims, puzzle games, etc.

I am still thrilled with my Steam Link and am using it everyday. With the current sale on both the Link and the Steam Controller, now is the time to grab one if you've been on the fence. The Link has been working great for me--just remember that you really need some kind of wired connection (I use powerline ethernet adapters).
Steam Controller review (and Steam Link update)

So are there any circumstance where you would say that the steam controller outperforms an xbone or ps4 controller?

You ask a tough question--primarily because up until recently I've ONLY used an XBox One controller (and I've never been great with that one). The Steam Controller has more buttons than the XBox One, but I don't think that makes it better (at least not for me) because just how many buttons are you going to be mashing? I guess if you're hardcore, having the extra buttons would be awesome--but for me, that feature doesn't add a lot of value. I don't have a PS4 so I can't comment on those controllers, but the XBox One controller is very comfortable in my hand, and everything is laid out on it in a useful way. I might just be too used to the XBox scheme, but the Steam Controller design doesn't seem as good. The controller handles turn upwards (while both the PS4 and XBox go down). The ABXY buttons are small and I find them a bit awkwardly placed. The large, touch-pad D-pad on the left hand side of the Steam Controller is about useless--not that it doesn't work, but no games I've played use it. It's an odd choice because it takes up so much real-estate on the gamepad, but none of the configs I've used have employed it. The main touchpad on the right has proved hard for me to master--I suspect a 12 year old kid with mad skills would prefer the Steam Controller over a traditional gamepad--but the learning curve is too high for me.

So back to your question about it "outperforming" console controllers...it theoretically could IF you really practiced on it and if you had a solid key binding set up. One reason I'm a PC gamer is that I do enjoy fast-twitch FPSs and I would NEVER want to play those with a gamepad--even on my console. I played through Tomb Raider on the XBox One recently and I found that okay mostly because it isn't a really fast game. I can see the Steam Controller handling something like that better than a traditional gamepad. But stuff like Doom would just suck (for me at least) on ANY type of controller. The two biggest selling points for the Steam Controller (IMHO) are the custom key bindings and the integration with the Link and Steam. If I had a wireless console controller (Xbox 360 or PS4) that worked with the Link then the decision to get a Steam Controller is tough--especially at the normal price of $50. Since I only have an XBox One controller and I'd need to buy other stuff to get it to work wirelessly, it just made more sense to spend the $35 on a Steam Controller on sale.

I don't think anyone would prefer a controller for any fast twitch fps games of they've ever used a keyboard and mouse set up before. Those will always be dominated by keyboard and mouse and I don't ever imagine myself making the transition to a controller for them.

That said, when it comes to any sort of platforms or fighting game I'll take a controller over keyboard and mouse any day.

I typically find myself addicted to one or two fps games at a time where I'll use my keyboard and mouse but I like to break up the monotony with other genres that I often feel would be better with a standard controller. I'm just hesitant with the track pads and only one analog stick.

I can't speak for fighting games, but for platformers the Steam Controller is sweet. I just noticed that Amazon now has it on sale too--so if you're a Prime member it'll be cheaper that way since Valve charges something like $6 or 7 for shipping.

Since you're already cool with using a controller, if you can spare the cash I'd get one. Worst case is you either return it or sell it on Craigslist. You'll probably end up liking it though.

1. Way more customisation options for games that don't support a controller. You can not only set the buttons and axes, but also different combinations for partial trigger press vs full press, emulate analog stick, etc.
  2. The pads can act as a trackball. Practice it a bit and it can be almost as good as a mouse. Hell, I play dota 2 with a trackball just fine (trash tier, though).
  3. The bumpers on the back are pretty awesome. More input available when you need to keep your thumbs on the analog controls.

Do note that it only work with steam games and there is no good alternative for a proper dpad.

I'm curious, does the Link introduce a lot of latency (both display and input lag)?

Not if you have a wired connection. I use a powerline ethernet adapter and the experience is generally flawless, HOWEVER I did experience some stuttering one day when my adapters started acting up. I flashed new firmware on them and everything was fine after that. I'm actually surprised at how well the Steam Controller works with the Link--after all, it's not connected to my remote gaming rig so it's having to wirelessly communicate with the Link, then the Link has to send my inputs back to the computer--but that is smooth as silk.

Re the sensitivity issue; the sensitivity of the mouse input on the right pad is linked not only to the sensitivity in the Steam controller settings, but in the game's mouse speed setting, which again is also tied to the OS's mouse speed setting. So there are three separate settings you can tinker with to get it feeling right.
good review--I've been wondering how people have been liking them since release.

I've had a Steam Controller since launch, and I'm still finding cool new ways to use it. It's my favorite gamepad, but I have to admit I wasn't very impressed with it at first, but the longer I used it, the more my view changed.

I love my Steam Link and usually when I'm using my Steam Controller, that's what I'm using. I use it for a lot more than just games, but I do sometimes use it with my tower when I'm not seated at the desk. I have a large screen and my bed is nearby, so sometimes I'll play from there using it, not often though. I do use it that way pretty often to play media or watch videos online though.

I rarely use my Xbox controller anymore with anything on my PC. The only time I do is for games that I can't get it to work for, a few sorted GoG games mostly, notably Witcher 2.

Normally, I use a KB and Mouse for gaming when I'm actually sitting next to my tower at the desk and it won't replace that, but once I adjusted to it, it's definitely preferable in all circumstances to an Xbox style pad, or even a PS4 controller.

This didn't happen immediately though. I used it for a month adjusting to it and figuring out how to tweak it for various games. After I did so, I don't really want to go back and my Xbox pad is basically a last resort for the rare times I just can't get it to work with something.

Some tips:

Learn to use the gyro settings. Seriously, this is more useful than you think. A lot of FPS games I put the x axis on the touchpad and use the gyros for y axis up down aiming. This works better for some games than others, but really helps a lot with FPS accuracy. Take the time to fine tune things and find the sweet spot for sensitivity, it's worth it.

The grip pads are amazing. I love those things. I usually map jump and crouch to them myself, but there are a lot of ways to use them some like to map things like iron sights or a flashlight function to them as well.

Consider mapping keyboard controls to the controller rather than using the X-input settings when possible. It opens up the pad's configuration a lot more. Some games allow for a hybrid between the two, which is very nice.

Make use of the num pad function for the left touch pad. It does take some getting used to, but really opens up hot key functions.

Learn to use Action Sets. This switches what the buttons do depending on the context of what you're doing in a game. You can set the controller up so that it behaves differently when you're in menus than when you're in gameplay. This works better in some games than others, but is a really great feature.

Mode switching, another thing that is very useful. Assign a button to alter how the controller behaves. This is especially useful in games that have a lot of button inputs. One of the shoulder buttons works best for this in my experience. Can be set to toggle or hold based on personal preference.

Edge Detect and Edge Spin are also very cool features that take some adjusting to, but also really improve using the controller once you adjust. Edge detect is especially useful for sprinting using WASD controls for example, just add a dual input command to the edges that ties shift to the movement keys. Edge spin is similar and lets the outer portion of the pad provide continuous mouse movement in a particular direction so you're not constantly swiping and lifting your thumb back to recenter.

The thing about the Steam Controller is that you've got to delve into the settings and tweak a lot. There are configurations you can get that other people have set up, but you'll still want to make personal adjustments to these most of the time.

You've also got to give it time. It's not a device you can just pick up and be good with immediately. It takes practice and has a learning curve. It's a much more complicated device than it seems on the surface, which is a positive and a negative at the same time.

Steam Controller is a seriously amazingly versatile game controller. It's not immediately apparent and seems awkward when you first use it, but after you adjust to it, it's definitely superior to a standard gamepad. The thing is, you've got to put in the time to adjust and learn how to set it up to suit you, you need to learn what the features do and how to tweak them to maximize it's effectiveness. It doesn't take all that long, honestly no more time than someone first learning how to use an X-input pad really.

A lot of people think that was easier for them than it really was at first because they've grown so used to using one that it's pretty much second nature. Steam controller is far more different from using that interface style than it first seems. You can 'plug and play' with it and it will work, but to get the most out of it you have to experiment and learn how it works and spend some time getting used to how to use it properly.

Once you get the hang of things, I doubt you'll really want to keep using a normal gamepad for most games.

Though, again, it's not a replacement for a KB and Mouse interface either, but a really good medium between that and a gamepad with a lot more functionality than an X-input pad has.

EDIT: A couple more tips:

Buy a four pack of rechargeable AA batteries and a charger. Never run out of power again, don't ever worry about having to use the USB chord to use it, and save some money in the process. When one pair runs dry, I immediately switch them out and plug the dead pair in to charge up.

Play with the trackball settings on the mouse touchpad. On 'medium' giving it a good swipe and letting it 'spin' turns you 90 degrees. Having it turned all the way up works well for some games, but others lower settings are better. Experiment. High is very loose and can be less accurate, low is very tight and might not be enough, and sometimes medium is not quite enough of a turn.

Wow, thanks for all the tips. You're 100% right...the biggest value in the controller is the unlimited amount of customization available. I'll set aside some time to poke around and learn how to do some of that stuff. That said, the take-away for other folks still reading this thread is that the Steam Controller is good/adequate straight out of the box, but is much move versatile (and powerful) IF you're willing to take the time to learn how to customize it fully.

TBH, I'm not how I feel about that. Console controllers are fairly dumbed down for a reason--if nothing else it keeps all players on equally bad footing. The Steam Controller reflects the flexibility inherent in PC gaming and provides a ton of options that can be a bit intimidating and overwhelming. As a vanilla controller just using the defaults it is OK, but it sounds like it really shines if you invest some time into it. Either way, at $35 on sale, it's worth picking one up.
